newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jobless rise puts Bonn forecasts in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Jobless rise puts Bonn forecasts in doubt.

text.p: German unemployment rose by 56,000 in May to a seasonally adjusted 4.358 million, the government said Friday, casting doubt about its own optimistic economic forecasts that are crucial for the contry to qualify for European monetary union.
The Federal Labour Office said the unemployment rate, which is based on unadjusted data, fell to 11.1 percent from 11.3 percent in April.
After releasing the figures, an official of the Labour Office said he could no longer endorse th government's unemployment forecast for this year.
"I believe the target figure of 3.95 million (average) jobless for 1997 is no longer attainable," Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda told a news conference.
"The seasonal revival in the German jobs market stopped in May. As before, the driving forces of the economy are insufficient to bring about a turnaround in the jobs market," Jagoda said.
Based on data for the first five months of the year, average unemployment could climb as high as 4.29 million, Gerhard Kleinhenz, head of the Labour Office's research institute, said.
He said the estimate was based on an assumption of 2.25 percent economic gorwth -- below the Bonn government's official forecast of 2.5 percent.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing called the jobs data "more than disappointing."
Higher unemployment would force Bonn to spend more than expected on jobless benefits at a time when it already expects an 18 billion mark ($10.4 billion) shortfall in tax revenue.

The yawning deficit has forced Finance Minister Theo Waigel to scramble for new sources of revenue and precipitated an embarrassing clash with the Bundesbank about revaluating Germany's gold and currency reserves.

"It is now increasingly clear that Theo Waigel will be unable to bring Germany's budget deficit down to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year," HSBC James Capel economist Stephen James said in a research note.
To qualify for the start of economic and monetary union in 1999, member nations are supposed to have total public deficits of no more than 3 percent of gross domestic product.
